Executive summary

Women victims of trafficking from Nigeria form a particular social group (PSG).

In general, a woman who has previously been trafficked is unlikely to be at risk of abuse, reprisals and/or discrimination on return that are sufficiently serious by their nature or repetition to amount to persecution or serious harm, solely on account of having previously been trafficked.

In general, a woman is unlikely to be at real risk of being re-trafficked on return solely on account of having previously been trafficked.

However, a woman may be at risk of abuse and/or re-trafficking amounting to persecution or serious harm depending on her particular circumstances and vulnerability. Factors which may increase vulnerability include, but are not limited to:

outstanding debts owed to traffickers or others who financed the journey

family or community involvement in the trafficking

the absence of a supportive family or social support network

social stigma or family rejection

poverty, destitution or lack of sustainable income

limited education, vocational skills or employment opportunities

mental health conditions or psychological trauma arising from trafficking experiences

In general, a victim of trafficking who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state actor and/or a non-state actor is likely to be able to obtain protection from the state. However, the effectiveness of protection remains uneven. Corruption, official complicity in trafficking offences, inadequate funding, weaknesses in victim identification, limited shelter capacity and shortcomings within the criminal justice system may hamper protection in some cases. The onus is on the person to demonstrate that they cannot obtain protection.

Where a woman has a well-founded fear of persecution as a victim of trafficking, whether she is able to relocate to escape that risk depends on her particular circumstances. In the country guidance case of HD (Trafficked women) Nigeria (CG) [2016] UKUT 454 (IAC), heard 18 to 20 July 2016 and promulgated 17 October 2016, the Upper Tribunal held that a woman who discloses characteristics of vulnerability that are indicative of a real risk of being trafficked, internal relocation is unlikely to be a viable alternative. There are not very strong grounds supported by cogent evidence to justify a departure from these findings. The onus is on decision makers to demonstrate that internal relocation is reasonable (or not unduly harsh) having regard to the individual circumstances of the person.

Where a claim is refused, it is unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 07 September 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights laws and policies, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

a person faces a real risk of persecution/serious harm by non-state actors because they are a victim of trafficking

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution/serious harm

a claim, if refused, it is unlikely to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

1.2 Modern slavery

1.2.1 Decision makers must note that guidance for competent authority staff in any part of the UK who make decisions on whether or not a person is a potential victim/victim of modern slavery for the purpose of the National Referral Mechanism is set out in the Modern Slavery: Statutory Guidance for England and Wales (under s49 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015) and non-statutory guidance for Scotland and Northern Ireland. The guidance is also aimed at staff within public authorities who may encounter potential victims of modern slavery and/or who are involved in supporting victims.

1.2.2 Decision makers also must note that if a person has a ‘positive conclusive grounds’ decision, a grant of permission to stay as a victim of human trafficking or slavery by the competent authorities may be considered.

1.2.3 For further information, see Temporary permission to stay for victims of human trafficking or slavery.

1.3 Assessing weight of ‘reasonable or conclusive grounds’ decisions

1.3.1 The reported case of DC (trafficking: protection/human rights appeals) Albania [2019] UKUT 00351 (IAC), heard 7 June 2019 and promulgated on 3 September 2019, referencing Secretary of State for the Home Department v MS (Pakistan) [2018] EWCA Civ 594, provides guidance on the weight to attach to a conclusive grounds decision made by a competent authority in an asylum or human rights case, and the order in which the Tribunal would consider overlapping asylum and MS claims.

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Women who have been trafficked form a particular social group (PSG) in Nigeria within the meaning of the Refugee Convention because they share an innate characteristic or a common background that cannot be changed or share a characteristic or belief that is so fundamental to identity or conscience that a person should not be forced to renounce it and have a distinct identity in Nigeria because the group is perceived as being different by the surrounding society.

3.1.2 Although women who have been trafficked form a PSG, establishing such membership is not sufficient to be recognised as a refugee. The question to be addressed is whether the person has a well-founded fear of persecution on account of their membership of such a group.

3.1.3 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds, see the Asylum Instruction, Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

4. Risk

4.1.1 In general, a woman who has previously been trafficked is unlikely to be at risk of abuse, reprisals and/or discrimination on return that are sufficiently serious by their nature or repetition to amount to persecution or serious harm, solely on account of having previously been trafficked. In general, a woman is unlikely to be at real risk of being re-trafficked on return solely on account of having previously been trafficked. However, a woman may be at risk of abuse and/or re-trafficking amounting to persecution or serious harm depending on her particular circumstances and vulnerability. Factors which may increase vulnerability include, but are not limited to:

outstanding debts owed to traffickers or others who financed the journey

prior threats or intimidation by traffickers

family or community involvement in the trafficking

particularly in cases of trafficking for sexual exploitation, an expectation of financial reward for the family, whether or not they were complicit in the original trafficking

the absence of a supportive family willing to accept the person on return

social stigma, rejection or ostracism by family or community members

lack of a social support network

poverty, destitution or lack of sustainable income

limited education, vocational skills or employment opportunities

mental health conditions or psychological trauma arising from trafficking experiences

inadequate access to reintegration support and assistance

4.1.2 Each case must be considered on its individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

4.1.3 Human trafficking affects men, women and children in Nigeria, although women and girls continue to comprise most identified victims, particularly in cases involving sexual exploitation. Victims commonly come from poor, marginalised or otherwise vulnerable backgrounds. Trafficking occurs both within Nigeria and across international borders for a range of exploitative purposes (see Prevalence and Profile of victims of trafficking).

4.1.4 Victims of trafficking commonly leave Nigeria in search of improved economic opportunities, employment, education or a better standard of living. Sources indicate that traffickers exploit these aspirations through false job offers, fraudulent recruitment schemes, deceptive promises of education or training, and offers to facilitate travel abroad. Some victims may start by paying for their travel, before being exploited or trapped into debt bondage by traffickers. Recruitment can take place in shops or markets, but victims are also identified and recruited online, particularly on social media platforms. Poverty, lack of economic opportunities, family and community pressure, displacement and limited educational opportunities are among the factors which may increase vulnerability to recruitment for trafficking. Victims may be exploited during transit or upon arrival in destination countries (see Profile of victims of trafficking, Traffickers’ profile and Traffickers’ strategies).

4.1.5 Trafficking is often facilitated through personal and community networks, including family members, community members and individuals in religious settings. Organised criminal groups are also among the main actors involved. Corrupt government officials and security officers may facilitate transit in exchange for bribes or sexual acts or sexually exploit victims in settings such as government-run IDP camps, informal camps and local communities (see Traffickers’ profile).

4.1.6 Victims are coerced and controlled at various stages of the trafficking process by means such as intimidation through juju (black magic), physical, psychological or sexual abuse, false promises, denial of basic needs, threats to the victim or family, debt bondage, withholding of wages, withholding of documents and blackmail, including ‘sextortion’. Traffickers sometimes use technology to monitor or restrict victims’ movements (see Means of coercion and control).

4.1.7 Victims of trafficking may face reprisals on return to Nigeria, particularly where debts remain unpaid, where victims have escaped their traffickers, or where they have cooperated with law enforcement. Reprisals may take the form of threats, intimidation, psychological pressure, family pressure linked to debt repayment, and, in some reported cases, physical violence. Traffickers may also target families. Sources indicate that fear of reprisals is common amongst victims, although the extent to which reprisals occur in practice is unclear (see Reprisals).

4.1.8 The experience of returnee victims of trafficking varies, with some receiving support from family and communities, while others experience stigma, rejection and pressure linked to societal expectations and financial obligations. Women, particularly those perceived to have engaged in prostitution or who return with children, are more likely to face social stigma, including negative impacts on marriage prospects and community acceptance. Family members may also pressure returnees to repay money invested in migration or expected earnings (see Reprisals and Family/social attitudes and treatment).

4.1.9 Women’s trafficking-related health conditions, which may include untreated sexually-transmitted infections, reproductive injuries and mental health difficulties, are reportedly viewed as shameful matters to be concealed rather than legitimate medical needs, and trauma-informed healthcare and psychological support are lacking (see Family/social attitudes and treatment).

4.1.10 Some returnees remain vulnerable to re-trafficking and re-exploitation. Factors that may increase vulnerability include poverty, limited educational attainment, unemployment, debt, family rejection, social stigma, inadequate reintegration support, and continuing contact with traffickers. Sources suggest that some returnees seek to migrate again because of economic hardship and pressure to support dependants. However, the availability of family support, livelihood opportunities, accommodation and reintegration assistance may reduce vulnerability (see Re-trafficking). See the guidance on Internal relocation, below, for an assessment of support services.

4.1.11 In the country guidance case of HD (Trafficked women) Nigeria (CG) [2016] UKUT 454 (IAC), heard 18 to 20 July 2016 and promulgated 17 October 2016, the Upper Tribunal (UT) found that previous guidance on trafficking set out in paragraphs 191 to 192 of PO (Trafficked Women) Nigeria CG [2009] UKAIT 00046 should no longer be followed (paragraph 187).

4.1.12 The UT in HD found that, for a person who was initially trafficked for the purpose of domestic servitude, even if they lived outside a state or NGO shelter, there ‘is unlikely to be an adverse risk from her original trafficker. There is no outstanding debt to be paid. Whether or not her original trafficker is successfully prosecuted will make no difference … Generally, there is no real risk of re-trafficking by reason alone of having been previously trafficked. But there may be a risk of trafficking by reason of her vulnerability.’ (paragraphs 148-149).

4.1.13 The UT added that, if she ‘… escaped from servitude, generally there would be no continuing interest by the trafficker or the employer, but the possibility cannot be excluded in every case.’ (paragraph 150).

4.1.14 The UT went on to find that if a woman’s ‘family is supportive and takes the victim of trafficking back into the family of their own volition generally she will not face a real risk of future persecution.’ However, if the woman was unwilling or unable for good reason to go to her family, she may be vulnerable to abuse (paragraphs 151-152).

4.1.15 In relation to a person who was trafficked for the purpose of sexual exploitation who returns to Nigeria, the UT in HD distinguished between a person who had paid her ‘debt’ to her traffickers and those who had not (paragraph 154).

4.1.16 The UT found that a woman who had paid her debt was not likely to be of interest to her original traffickers and therefore she would generally not be at risk of reprisal or re-trafficking on return by reason alone of having been previously trafficked (although there may be a risk of trafficking by reason of ‘vulnerability’) (paragraphs 155-156).

4.1.17 However, there may, in some cases, be a real risk of serious harm from her family, whether or not they were initially complicit in her trafficking for sexual exploitation. The UT found that ‘It is generally reasonable to conclude that her family would expect an economic and financial return from her consequent upon her travel to Europe. Return to her previous trafficking situation under the duress of family pressure, family violence, ostracism and stigmatisation by her community and possible resultant destitution, homelessness and lack of any financial security is likely in most cases to amount to serious harm.’ (paragraph 157).

4.1.18 The UT, however, also held that a person who had an outstanding debt to her traffickers will be of some continuing interest to them, but this is most likely to be whilst the woman remains in Europe. Generally, neither the woman nor her family were likely to be at real risk of reprisal in Nigeria, although there may be ‘some individuals for whom that generality does not apply for example where the young woman has been threatened or her family has been threatened after she left the trafficker.’ (para 159 to 160).

4.1.19 The UT further found: ‘If the victim of trafficking were able to return to her family and they were both willing to accept her and able to provide her with appropriate support she would be unlikely to [be] re trafficked. The evidence before us does not support a finding that Nigerian traffickers, in general, resort to abduction (although that is not the case in the North East of Nigeria). ‘There may be some cases where the family pose a real risk. For example, if the young woman was close to paying off the debt, her family may require her to return to the trafficker to enable her to start sending money back to the family. Close links between victim and trafficker through family or community ties would result in her being identified as having returned home. There may be psychological and emotional pressure either for the victim to “voluntarily” return to her exploiters or she will simply be trafficked again.’ (paragraphs 163 to 164).

4.1.20 The UT found that in general, a woman who has been trafficked for sexual exploitation and returns to Nigeria is unlikely to be at risk of being re-trafficked by her original traffickers by reason alone of having been previously trafficked. However, that person may be at risk of abuse and/or being re-trafficked depending on her particular ‘vulnerability’ (paragraphs 165 to 166).

4.1.21 The UT went on to hold the following country guidance:

‘Although the Government of Nigeria recognises that the trafficking of women, both internally and transnationally, is a significant problem to be addressed, it is not established by the evidence that for women in general in Nigeria there is a real risk of being trafficked.

‘For a woman returning to Nigeria, after having been trafficked to the United Kingdom, there is in general no real risk of retribution or of being trafficked afresh by her original traffickers.

‘Whether a woman returning to Nigeria having previously been trafficked to the United Kingdom faces on return a real risk of being trafficked afresh will require a detailed assessment of her particular and individual characteristics. Factors that will indicate an enhanced risk of being trafficked include, but are not limited to:

‘a. The absence of a supportive family willing to take her back into the family unit;

b. Visible or discernible characteristics of vulnerability, such as having no social support network to assist her, no or little education or vocational skills, mental health conditions, which may well have been caused by experiences of abuse when originally trafficked, material and financial deprivation such as to mean that she will be living in poverty or in conditions of destitution;

c. The fact that a woman was previously trafficked is likely to mean that she was then identified by the traffickers as someone disclosing characteristics of vulnerability such as to give rise to a real risk of being trafficked. On returning to Nigeria, it is probable that those characteristics of vulnerability will be enhanced further in the absence of factors that suggest otherwise.

‘Factors that indicate a lower risk of being trafficked include, but are not limited to:

a. The availability of a supportive family willing to take the woman back into the family unit;

b. The fact that the woman has acquired skills and experiences since leaving Nigeria that better equip her to have access to a livelihood on return to Nigeria, thus enabling her to provide for herself.’ (paragraphs 188 to 191).

4.1.22 The CG case of HD was based on country evidence up to the first half of 2016. The country information in this note does not indicate that there are ‘very strong grounds supported by cogent evidence’ to justify a departure from these findings.

4.1.23 For further guidance on assessing risk, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

5. Protection

5.1.1 In general, a victim of trafficking who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state actor and/or a non-state actor is likely to be able to obtain protection from the state.

5.1.2 However, the effectiveness of protection remains uneven. Corruption, official complicity in trafficking offences, inadequate funding, weaknesses in victim identification, limited shelter capacity and shortcomings within the criminal justice system may hamper protection in some cases. As established in Horvath v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2000] UKHL 37, the state is not required to guarantee protection against every act of persecution. The existence of shortcomings within the protection system does not, in itself, demonstrate that the state is unwilling or unable to provide sufficient protection. Corruption, sympathy or weakness of some individuals in the justice system does not mean that the state is unwilling to afford protection, and there may be various sound reasons why criminals may not be brought to justice.

5.1.3 Each case must be decided on its individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate that they cannot obtain protection.

5.1.4 For general guidance on protection, see the Country Policy and Information Note Nigeria: Actors of protection.

5.1.5 Nigeria has ratified a number of international protocols and conventions to prevent and tackle trafficking in persons. Domestic legislation criminalises trafficking and there is a legal and institutional framework to prevent trafficking, prosecute offenders and support victims. The Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act, as amended in 2015, criminalises trafficking for sexual exploitation, forced labour and other forms of exploitation. The Act established the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), the lead agency responsible for anti-trafficking activities (see Legal and policy measures).

5.1.6 NAPTIP works alongside the Nigeria Police Force, Nigeria Immigration Service, state anti-trafficking task forces and other government agencies. It has responsibility for investigations, prosecutions, victim identification, protection and prevention activities. Sources report strong ongoing cooperation between NAPTIP and international partners, foreign law enforcement agencies and civil society organisations (see Enforcement agencies and activities and International cooperation).

5.1.7 The government continues to investigate, prosecute and convict traffickers and has established mechanisms for victim identification and referral. During the April 2024 to March 2025 reporting period covered by the US State Department’s (USSD) 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report, authorities investigated 744 trafficking cases, initiated prosecutions against 71 alleged traffickers and secured 49 convictions, representing an increase on the figures reported for 2024. However, data covering the period 2021 to 2025 fluctuates and does not indicate a sustained upward trend. While the increase recorded in 2025 may reflect improvements in enforcement or reporting, the available evidence does not establish the reasons for the increase or demonstrate that trafficking prevalence has risen. Enforcement data should therefore be considered alongside evidence relating to victim identification, access to protection, institutional capacity and the effectiveness of the criminal justice system (see Investigations, arrests, prosecutions and convictions).

5.1.8 Access to protection and assistance depends on a victim being identified or successfully self-referring to an appropriate organisation in Nigeria. Victims are identified and referred to protection services through NAPTIP and partner organisations. Screening efforts are reportedly inadequate among vulnerable populations such as internally displaced persons (IDPs) and women allegedly associated with non-armed state groups. In some cases, authorities detained or returned victims to their Boko Haram husbands and traffickers (see Victim identification and the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), Investigations, arrests, prosecutions and convictions and Effectiveness of agencies and criminal justice system).

5.1.9 The USSD assesses that, whilst the government is making significant efforts to combat trafficking, Nigeria does not fully meet the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking (see Action to combat trafficking). The report nevertheless notes over the April 2024 to March 2025 period that Nigeria increased investigations, prosecutions, victim identification, funding for victim protection and prevention activities compared to previous reporting periods. However, it does not explicitly explain the reasons for the increases in enforcement activity and victim identification (see Effectiveness of agencies and criminal justice system).

5.1.10 NAPTIP and partner organisations operate shelters and provide legal, medical, psychosocial, vocational and reintegration support to victims. However, shelter capacity is limited, and support may be constrained by funding and resource shortages. Sources also reported that some victims, particularly those returning outside assisted return programmes, may encounter difficulties accessing support services (see Shelters and assistance, Federal and state government support, International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and Non-governmental and religious organisations).

5.1.11 Accommodation options are not limited to NAPTIP shelters. In addition to shelters operated by NAPTIP and state authorities, victims may access support provided by non-governmental and religious organisations. Sources report that some NGO-operated shelters function on an open basis and do not restrict residents’ contact with the outside world. While this may afford greater freedom of movement, the same sources noted that such shelters may be less able to protect victims who fear reprisals from traffickers, and that victims requiring enhanced protection were generally referred to NAPTIP shelters. The availability and suitability of accommodation and support should therefore be considered in light of the individual’s circumstances and protection needs (see Shelters and assistance, Federal and state government support and Non-governmental and religious organisations). For location-specific information on shelters, see Internal relocation, below.

5.1.12 In the country guidance case of HD (Trafficked women) Nigeria CG [2016] UKUT 454 (IAC), the Upper Tribunal found that a trafficked woman would generally not be at risk whilst accommodated in a NAPTIP or NGO shelter, but that because that support would be likely to be temporary, her long-term position would require careful assessment on the facts of the individual case (paragraphs 141 to 142). The country information in this note does not indicate that there are ‘very strong grounds supported by cogent evidence’ to justify a departure from these findings.

5.1.13 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

6. Internal relocation

6.1.1 Where a woman has a well-founded fear of persecution as a victim of trafficking, whether she is able to relocate to escape that risk depends on her particular circumstances (see the CG case of HD and the assessment and background information in the Country Policy and Information Note Nigeria: Internal relocation).

6.1.2 The UT in HD found, in regard to women victims of trafficking:

‘For a woman who does face a real risk of being trafficked if she returns to her home area, the question of whether internal relocation will be available as a safe and reasonable alternative that will not be unduly harsh will require a detailed assessment of her particular circumstances. For a woman who discloses the characteristics of vulnerability described above [see section on Risk above] that are indicative of a real risk of being trafficked, internal relocation is unlikely to be a viable alternative.’ (paragraph 193).

6.1.3 The CG case of HD was based on country evidence up to the first half of 2016. The country information in this note does not indicate that there are ‘very strong grounds supported by cogent evidence’ to justify a departure from these findings.

6.1.4 While the onus is on the person to establish a well-founded fear of persecution or real risk of serious harm, the onus is on decision makers to demonstrate that internal relocation is reasonable (or not unduly harsh) having regard to the individual circumstances of the person.

6.1.5 NAPTIP operates shelters in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Lagos, Benin, Enugu, Sokoto, Uyo, Kano, Maiduguri, Osogbo, Ekiti, Yobe, Makurdi, Katsina and Ondo. Other state-run shelters operate in Lagos State and Benin City (Edo State). In Lagos State, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the Lagos State Government operate transit shelters where returnees may stay temporarily pending evacuation arrangements and onward travel. Various NGOs and faith-based organisations also provide shelter and support services. Most shelters available through government, civil society and international partners are for women and girls. In Abuja, the Women Trafficking and Child Labour Eradication Foundation (WOTCLEF) provides assistance to women, boys and girls who are victims of internal and transnational trafficking (see Shelters and assistance).

6.1.6 Support may be available to returnees and victims of trafficking through government, international and NGO programmes. Such support may include temporary accommodation, counselling, family tracing and reunification, skills acquisition and vocational training, and reintegration assistance (see Shelters and assistance and Process of return and initial support). In major urban centres such as Lagos and Abuja, support services are available through NAPTIP and NGO partners, and these locations may offer greater access to employment, education and support services than some other parts of the country. However, the available evidence indicates that reintegration support is not comprehensive and there is no centralised system for monitoring long-term reintegration outcomes (see the Country Policy and Information Note Nigeria: Actors of protection, Shelters and assistance and Re-trafficking).

6.1.7 For further guidance on internal relocation and factors to consider, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

7. Certification

7.1.1 Where a claim is refused, it is unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

7.1.2 For further guidance on certification, see Certification of Protection and Human Rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

8. Prevalence

8.1 General

8.1.1 The US Department of State’s 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report, dated 29 September 2025, covered the period April 2024 to March 2025 (USSD 2025 TiP report). In a section summarising government and civil society reporting on the nature and scope of trafficking over the previous 5 years, the report stated: ‘Trafficking affects all communities … Human traffickers exploit domestic and foreign victims in Nigeria, and traffickers exploit victims from Nigeria abroad. Internal trafficking is more prevalent … However, authorities identified Nigerian trafficking victims – often exploited by Nigerian traffickers – in countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.’[footnote 1]

8.1.2 IOM (International Organisation for Migration) Nigeria, in an article dated 24 September 2024 (2024 IOM Nigeria article), stated: ‘In 2023, an estimated 1.4 million Nigerians were involved in forced labour or sexual exploitation, with many trafficked within the country or to Europe …’[footnote 2]

convictions, see Investigations, arrests, prosecutions and convictions

returns, see Number of returns

8.2 Trafficking from Nigeria

8.2.1 IOM Nigeria, in their Profile of Nigerian Victims of Human Trafficking Since 2017, last updated 22 July 2024 (2024 IOM Nigeria report), featured a bar chart to show data collected by the IOM on the number of male (M) and female (F) victims trafficked from Nigeria and identified between 2017 and Quarter 1 of 2024. IOM Nigeria explained: ‘The data does not represent a sample of the underlying population … [The figures] are based on individuals identified as victims of trafficking, either by the IOM through case management, as part of a referral mechanism by the authorities, most often in the country of exploitation, or from frontline civil society organizations that work directly to assist victims of trafficking.’[footnote 3] The chart is reproduced below[footnote 4]:

8.2.2 Referring to the same cohort, the 2024 IOM Nigeria report stated: ‘… [F]orced labor, sexual exploitation, slavery, and begging collectively represent 98% of the reported types of exploitation. Across all categories of exploitation, women appear to be more susceptible. A significant number of women experienced forced labor and sexual exploitation. Additional forms of exploitation include forced marriage, illicit activities, begging, forced military service, and organ removal[.]’[footnote 5]

8.2.3 The ENACT (Enhancing Africa’s capacity to respond more effectively to transnational organised crime) project is implemented by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS, a pan-African civil society organisation[footnote 6]), INTERPOL and the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime (GI-TOC, an international civil society organisation[footnote 7]). In a report dated 13 June 2025 (2025 ENACT report), based on various sources, ENACT stated:

‘Open sources [of] information on African victims in Europe shows that Nigerian women are the most represented. As shown in the figure 4, in 2022, Nigeria was the main country of citizenship of non-EU victims in the EU, with 1,312 Nigerian citizens reported victims, most of which were women.

‘In France, according to the annual conclusions of NGOs in charge of assisting victims of trafficking, in 2022, 52 per cent of all victims of sexual exploitation were Nigerians, a stable figure compared to 2021.’[footnote 8]

8.2.4 The same ENACT report stated: ‘European countries have requested most INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions [international police alerts[footnote 9]] targeting West and North African offenders involved in sex trafficking, with a majority of these targeting Nigerian nationals. This suggests strong linkages between OCGs [organised crime groups] from these countries, notably Nigeria, and sex trafficking in Europe. Since 2021, there has been a decrease in INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions requested by European countries targeting individuals from Nigeria for trafficking in human beings and sexual exploitation, with the coincidental emergence of INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions targeting other West and North African nationals.

‘Some European countries also noted a decrease in arrests of Nigerian sex traffickers starting in 2021. This trend may be explained by the weakening of these OCGs due to an increased enforcement pressure. Alternatively, it may be attributed to a potential lack of detection, due to the adoption of new modi operandi.’[footnote 10]

8.2.5 The 2025 ENACT report further observed: ‘Several European countries noted a recent and ongoing decrease in the number of identified victims from Nigeria. In some country, it decreases by more than 80 per cent from 2021 to 2023 [sic].’[footnote 11] The report suggested the following possible explanations for the decrease in identified Nigerian victims:

a decrease in the overall number of migrants travelling via the Mediterranean route

a revocation in 2018 by the oba (religious leader) of Benin City of juju oaths binding victims to their traffickers

international cooperation and operations resulting in a reduction in trafficking

a ‘trend towards hidden prostitution’ since the Covid pandemic, in which case the decrease would represent a decline in detection rather than a reduction in the number of victims[footnote 12]

8.2.6 For more information on juju oaths and revocation by the oba, see Means of control and coercion.

‘Many actors are involved in trafficking, including family and community members, or individuals in religious settings. In the context of migration routes, actors involved in migrant smuggling may also engage in trafficking, either by collaborating with trafficking networks or by directly exploiting migrants themselves.

‘Trafficking networks exploit Nigerian victims in Europe, the Middle East (including the Gulf countries) mostly in sex trafficking and domestic servitude. Criminal groups, some linked to cults or confraternities … play a central role also in international trafficking.’[footnote 31]

9.1.2 The 2024 IOM Nigeria report stated that of the 4,261 Nigerian female victims of trafficking identified outside Nigeria between 2017 and Q1 2024, 46.6% were recruited by a friend or acquaintance, 8.9% by family or a relative and 44.5% by ‘others’[footnote 32]. 9.1.3 The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), in their Global Report on Trafficking in Persons 2024, dated December 2024 (2024 UNODC global trafficking report), cited research undertaken by the University of Amsterdam’s Sarah Adeyinka on the role of family members in trafficking from Nigeria (see page 91 of the 2024 UNODC report for the research methodology). It stated:

‘… [T]here were different types of family involvement, and family involvement did not always mean family approval of trafficking in persons. Three main groups emerged from the analysis:

‘In the first group, participants’ family members were part of the recruitment, and enforcement of exploitation …

‘In the second group, although family members were not explicitly pushing the participants to embark on the journey, they did not stop them and/or were supportive of the idea that they were going with a trafficker, as it meant some remittances would come their way.’[footnote 33]

[The third group were] ‘Family members who were aware of their children and wards traveling but were deceived, and thought it was for other purposes – vocational jobs, education, etc.’[footnote 34]

9.1.4 The 2025 EUAA country report stated:

‘Trafficking is often facilitated through personal and communal networks, and in some contexts, it is viewed not as exploitation but as a voluntary and viable path to economic and social advancement. Especially in Edo State, trafficking victims are often familiar with their traffickers, who are typically part of their community and perceived as ‘sponsors’ offering assistance in traveling abroad. Traffickers are often perceived not as criminals, but as business associates or migration agents, comparable to recruiters of professionals like doctors and nurses. As explained by Roland Nwoha, director at IRARA Nigeria [International Returns and Reintegration, an organisation that delivers reintegration assistance to returning migrants across Nigeria through local partner organisations[footnote 35]] most people do not recognise the criminal nature of trafficking: “some victims even view traffickers as saviours, as people who have come to rescue them from harsh economic conditions.”’[footnote 36]

9.1.5 The same EUAA report observed: ‘In January 2025, the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS) uncovered a sect in Kaduna State, Northwestern Nigeria, allegedly linked to trafficking in human beings’ activities. The group, known as ACHAD Life Mission International, is reported to promote the revival of African traditions and operates independently of any mainstream religion. Its leader, identified as Yokana, is based in Jos, Plateau State, an area recently classified as a human trafficking hotspot, particularly for cases involving the trafficking of children. According to authorities, more than 100 victims were rescued in Plateau State over the past year.’[footnote 37]

9.1.6 With regard to roles within the trafficking process, the Punch, a Nigerian privately-owned newspaper[footnote 38], in an article dated 14 July 2024 (2024 Punch roles article), explained:

‘In the world of trafficking, various individuals play crucial roles. Typically, the process begins with someone presenting an opportunity to vulnerable individuals. These victims are then linked to a key player known as the ‘Connection Man’ or ‘Border’ who facilitates the trafficking operation.

The Connection Man acts as an agent responsible for overseeing the victims’ travel arrangements and linking them with ‘Buyers’ overseas who financially support the victims. Investigations revealed that some Buyers cover the travel expenses of the victims to decrease the payment owed to the Connection Man upon the victims’ arrival. From the buyers who are referred to as madams or masters, the victims are either sold again to ‘Users’ or rented out for different purposes.’[footnote 39]

9.1.7 The 2025 EUAA country report stated: ‘During transport, ‘movement facilitators’ use bribery to bypass law enforcement, while ‘escorting traffickers’ (also called ‘Trolleys’ or ‘Coyotes’) maintain physical control over victims. ‘Logisticians’ arrange travel, and ‘migrant smugglers’ (some of whom exploit or sell victims) support with the movement across borders.’[footnote 40]

9.1.8 Regarding the definition of a trafficking ‘madam’, the University of Amsterdam’s Sarah Akeyinka, Ine Lietaert, associate professor at Ghent University, Belgium[footnote 41], and Ilse Derluyn, professor at Ghent University and director of the university’s Centre for the Social Study of Migration and Refugees[footnote 42], in a paper dated November 2023, based on various sources, reported:

‘In this phenomenon [trafficking of Nigerian women and girls overseas], a “madam” is a woman who was formerly trafficked but stayed with the trafficking network … [T]hey are usually at the top of the trafficking hierarchy, and they control the girls and women working for them. Madams organize victims’ recruitment, they collude with government officials and smugglers to secure passage for victims, and they ensure that the victims work in prostitution after arrival in the destination country. They don’t do this on their own, but collaborate with extensive criminal networks.’[footnote 43]

9.1.9 The 2025 ENACT report observed:

‘Austrian police noted that Nigerian OCGs in Europe are managed by ‘Madams,’ who are high ranking members of Nigerian sex trafficking OCGs. Some of them travel between Nigeria and Europe and have several Nigerian victims forced to work for them. Their victims often reside in different European countries. The ‘Madams’ use Nigerian OCGs member [sic] to monitor the victims during the transport from Nigeria and during the exploitation phase in Europe.’[footnote 44]

9.1.10 Regarding ‘baby factories’ and their operators, the USSD 2025 TiP report stated: ‘Illicit actors operate “baby factories” – often disguised as orphanages, maternity homes, or religious centers – where traffickers hold women against their will, rape them, and force them to carry and deliver a child. They then sell the children, sometimes with the intent of exploiting them in forced labor and sex trafficking.’[footnote 45]

9.1.11 The Nation, a Nigerian privately-owned newspaper[footnote 46], in an article dated 19 January 2026 (2026 Nation article), quoted a statement issued by NAPTIP Director General Binta Bello as saying that among the high-profile traffickers convicted or pursued by NAPTIP in 2025 ‘were some popular operators and care homes across the country whose alleged nefarious activities were busted …’[footnote 47]

9.1.12 In relation to northern Nigeria, the USSD 2025 TiP report stated: ‘These non-state armed groups [Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISIS-WA or ISWAP)] continue to abduct women and girls in the northern regions of Nigeria, many of whom they exploit in forced labor, including in domestic servitude, and in sexual slavery … Boko Haram punishes girls, including for refusing to marry, by forcing them to be suicide bombers … Criminal gangs in the south recruit and use children in forced criminality, including kidnappings and robberies, and exploit them in sex trafficking. 9.1.13 The same USSD report further stated: ‘Reports indicate government officials, as well as security officers, have sexually exploited victims in government-run IDP camps, informal camps, and local communities, including around Maiduguri … During a previous reporting period, an NGO alleged soldiers sexually exploited female detainees in a Borno State military detention center.’[footnote 49]

9.2 Traffickers’ strategies

9.2.1 With reference to recruitment methods in West and North Africa in general, the 2025 ENACT report stated: ‘… [O]ffenders use fraudulent and deceptive schemes to recruit the victims both online and offline. The main reported methods include: fake advertisements for opportunities abroad, such as well-paid jobs, false immigration offers to Europe, and study opportunities … According to information provided by Austrian police, traffickers offer fraudulent job offers as nannies and receptionists in Austria or other parts of Europe …

‘To lure the victims online, recruiters mainly use fake identities on mainstream social networks and messaging applications such as WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram, Messenger, Snapchat, Tik Tok, Telegram or Instagram. OCGs in Africa use social media to improve their social engineering schemes: they study the profiles of potential victims to tailor their messages to recruit victims online.’[footnote 50]

9.2.2 The same ENACT report observed that online recruitment of victims has been increasing, adding: ‘According to Europol, “most victims are identified and recruited via the Internet, particularly on social media platforms”.’[footnote 51] Offline recruitment ‘generally takes place through intermediaries … Nigerian women are also often recruited at markets or shops.’[footnote 52]

9.2.3 The 2024 Punch roles article reported: ‘… Throughout the entirety of the trafficking chain, spanning from the initial referrer to the Connection Man, Buyer, and ultimately the User, devious tactics are employed to keep the victims unaware of the imminent danger they are facing.’[footnote 53]

9.2.4 The 2024 UNODC global trafficking report stated: ‘Working on or with family members is a tactical strategy used by traffickers who understand the key aspects of respecting and obeying elders in the Nigerian society, and use that to their advantage.’[footnote 54]

9.2.5 The USSD 2025 TiP report observed:

‘Traffickers increasingly use social media to identify and recruit potential victims. Media and NGOs report unscrupulous actors, including Russian officials and illicit recruiters, fraudulently recruited women ages 18-22 from Africa – including Nigeria – … for vocational training programs and subsequently placed them in military drone production sites. Media report workers at these sites are subjected to hazardous conditions, surveillance, hour and wage violations, contract switching, and worker-paid recruitment fees, all of which are indicators of human trafficking.’[footnote 55]

‘“Young women are often under enormous pressure to provide for their families or to escape an abusive environment. 10. Returns process and initial support

10.1 Number of returns

10.1.1 The 2024 IOM Nigeria report stated: ‘Between 2017 and Q1 2024, IOM facilitated the voluntary return of 4,877 Victims of Trafficking (VOTs) holding Nigerian citizenship, among whom 616 (13%) were male and 4261 (87%) [were female].’[footnote 129]

10.1.2 The same IOM Nigeria report stated with reference to both male and female victims of trafficking that ‘… although Libya records the highest voluntary return of VOTs, … Mali has the highest number of child victims returned to Nigeria over the course of 7 years consistently outweigh[ing] that of adult victims’[footnote 130].

10.1.3 The 2024 Punch roles article reported:

‘On June 14, the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission disclosed that it rescued 10 teenage girls who were trafficked to Ghana for prostitution and brought them back to Nigeria.

‘The Director of Media and Public Relations and Protocols of the Commission, Abdur-Rahman Balogun, during an interview with our correspondent on July 1 said, “Because of its vital role, concerned Nigerians invite us to help them out whenever there are Nigerians stranded or trafficked for shameful deals.

‘“We involve our embassies or High Commissions and equally use the Nigerians Diaspora Organisation in that particular country to get us the necessary information and facilitate repatriation before handing them back to relevant agencies. We have rescued a lot of Nigerians, especially youths through that process.”’[footnote 131]

10.1.4 The 2025 EUAA report stated with reference to male and female returnees in general: ‘Since October 2022, IOM has supported the voluntary return of over 20 970 Nigerian migrants under the MPRR-SSA [Migrant Protection, Return and Reintegration Programme for Sub-Saharan Africa], primarily from Libya and Niger.’[footnote 132]

10.2 Process of return and initial support

10.2.1 Citing the EUAA’s July 2025 online interview with Sarah Adeyinka of the University of Amsterdam, the 2025 EUAA report stated: ‘Individuals return to Nigeria through three main ways: forced return, self-funded or family-funded return, and assisted return through IOM’s AVRR [Assisted Voluntary Return and Reintegration] programmes.’[footnote 133]

10.2.2 The USSD 2025 TiP report stated: ‘NAPTIP’s Protocol for Identification, Safe Return and Rehabilitation of Trafficked Persons provided formal procedures for authorities assisting victims exploited abroad upon identification and during and after repatriation.’[footnote 134]

10.2.3 Referring to Nigerian male and female victims of trafficking whose voluntary return to Nigeria was facilitated by the IOM between 2017 and Q1 2024, the 2024 IOM Nigeria report stated:

‘Following their return, IOM, in collaboration with key governmental entities, civil society organizations, and non-governmental actors, facilitated their reception and support. Upon arrival, immediate assistance, including medical care for individuals with varying degrees of health conditions, and psychosocial counseling aimed at fostering emotional, social, and cognitive capacities necessary for reintegration into the community, were provided. 10.2.4 Ngozi L Uzomah, Ignatius I Madu, Chukwuedozie K Ajaero and Eberechukwu J Ezea, of the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, in Enugu State, wrote a working paper (Uzomah and others 2024), dated 28 November 2024, on Nigerian migrants, including victims of trafficking, returning from North Africa, as part of the GAPs Horizon Europe project on migrant returns[footnote 136]. ‘During the early stage of their return at the airport, Nigerian government agencies await the migrants to welcome them as part of the return and reintegration process. ‘Meet & Greet at the airport.

11.1.1 The USSD 2025 TiP report stated that although the law prohibited the penalisation of trafficking victims for association with non-state armed groups and other unlawful acts committed as a direct result of being trafficked,

‘… observers reported the government arrested and, in some cases, inappropriately detained for prolonged periods women and children removed from or allegedly associated with Boko Haram and ISIS-West Africa (ISIS-WA), including trafficking victims. ‘One NGO report highlighted two cases in which sharia courts fined girls who had escaped Boko Haram for refusing to return to their husbands to whom they had been forcibly married.’[footnote 140]

12. Treatment by non-state actors after return

12.1 Reprisals

12.1.1 There was limited recent information on reprisals, in the sources consulted for this note (see Bibliography).

12.1.2 The Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), in their ‘General Country of Origin Information Report Nigeria’, dated January 2023 (Dutch MoFA 2023 report), stated:

‘All sources consulted stated that victims of human trafficking are at risk of reprisals. Possible reasons for this are that they have not yet paid off their debts, or in order to prevent the victim from assisting with the prosecution of traffickers and smugglers. According to a confidential source, human smuggling and trafficking networks from Nigeria, more than those from other countries, are closely interconnected from the start to the end of the route. The exploiter abroad is usually in contact, directly or indirectly, with the victim’s family. This makes it more difficult for the victims to escape the smugglers and traffickers. In addition, human smugglers and traffickers are often powerful and wealthy people, sometimes even with political backing …

‘Many female trafficking victims from southern Nigeria have a great fear of supernatural reprisals if they flee sexual exploitation in Europe before paying off their debt …

‘Most of the reprisals against trafficker victims were psychological and emotional in nature, through fear resulting from the juju oath and pressure from family members. Because it was not clear exactly what consequences would arise from breaking the oath, the victims and those around them attributed to it every misfortune that they experienced. In their eyes, these were therefore real, physical reprisals. The fear that resulted from a juju oath was generally very effective. Physical reprisals were therefore rarely necessary. Human traffickers sometimes used their connections to physically threaten and harass victims, for example in order to recover incriminating evidence or to prevent the victim from testifying. Cult members were also used for this purpose …’[footnote 141]

12.1.3 The same Dutch MoFA report observed: ‘According to confidential sources, protection against reprisals is inadequate, given that victims do not provide information to the authorities out of fear and the smugglers often have powerful connections and the means to bribe the authorities.’[footnote 142]

12.1.4 The Dutch MoFA published an explanatory note, dated 21 March 2024 (2024 Dutch MoFA note), which they explained was to supplement and clarify, but not replace, their 2023 report[footnote 143]. The note, based on various sources including consultations with 2 new anonymous sources, stated:

‘According to various sources, victims of human trafficking faced reprisals or the threat of reprisals. In addition to reprisals from human traffickers and/or their accomplices, victims might also face reprisals from their own family members, friends or partners … There are no known studies on the extent to which reprisals take place. In many cases, victims did not communicate about reprisals (or the threat thereof) out of fear …

‘Reprisals could result from situations in which human traffickers or others [sic] parties involved in human trafficking (e.g. family members, friends or partners) had invested resources in the victim’s journey and deemed that the victim still owed them money. According to several confidential sources, the vast majority of the victims had high debts upon return. In this regard, a distinction could be drawn between victims who still owed money to human traffickers, and others who were in debt to friends and/or family. For example, there were cases in which relatives or acquaintances had advanced money for the journey, or had even been the ones who had made the deal with the human trafficker. There were also cases in which family and friends had been forced to pay ransom, thereby shifting the debt from the human traffickers to the family and friends. According to one confidential source, it was probably more common for human traffickers to invest in the journeys of women than it was for them to invest in the journeys of men. This was because women were expected to earn the money back for the human trafficker through prostitution. No research has been done on this, however, and there are no statistics available on it …

‘One confidential source spoke of two scenarios regarding debt. In cases where the victim had been intercepted en route by the police or coastguard, human traffickers were often sympathetic to the victim’s inability to pay the debt immediately. According to this source, however, in cases where victims had decided to flee and return home on their own, human traffickers or madams would do everything they could to recoup their investment. The source noted that “everything” could include physical abuse or murder. More commonly, however, victims were held captive by the police or third parties, acting at the behest of human traffickers, until their debts were paid in full …

‘In addition to reprisals due to financial debts, confidential sources reported that human traffickers could also proceed with reprisals to prevent victims from reporting or otherwise cooperating with criminal proceedings against human traffickers, or out of revenge because victims had cooperated with prosecution.’[footnote 144]

12.1.5 The 2024 MoFA note also reported:

‘There were known cases of physical reprisals. According to confidential sources, physical reprisals at the behest of human traffickers occasionally occurred. These physical reprisals could range from kidnapping (for ransom) and drugging, to the assault and killing of victims or their loved ones. One confidential source provided the example of a victim of human trafficking who had returned to Nigeria from another country in the region. The victim had initially gone abroad with the cooperation of the father and an aunt, who hoped that she would earn money for the family. The victim’s mother, who had not known about the agreement, was physically assaulted by the human trafficker for cooperating in the victim’s return to Nigeria … [A confidential source] provided the example of a human trafficker who had been ordered by the court to pay hefty compensation to a victim. A week after the verdict, the victim was shot dead in the street. The source reported being aware of several similar cases.

‘According to confidential sources, the risk of physical reprisals increased with the amount of financial debt. This could be because the human trafficker had invested more money in the victim’s journey; because the victim had been unwilling or unable (e.g. due to illness) to carry out the work imposed; and/or because the victim had fled the human trafficker (in many cases, a madam) before the debt was paid off. According to the same sources, the risk also increased if the human trafficker was not a close connection to the victim.’[footnote 145]

12.1.6 Regarding non-physical reprisals, the same Dutch MoFA note stated:

‘… [T]here were threats by human traffickers — even if they did not lead to physical violence — and pressure from the family to pay off debts, which were perceived as emotional reprisals. According to several sources, there was a great fear amongst victims of human trafficking concerning what could happen if they did not comply with the wishes of the human trafficker. It should be kept in mind that the victims had often already faced high levels of violence during their smuggling and exploitation. The threats were thus highly credible.’[footnote 146]

12.1.7 For more information on family pressure to repay debts, see Family/social attitudes and treatment.

12.1.8 The same Dutch MoFA note further reported:

‘Confidential sources also spoke of spiritual attacks. This was in reference to misfortune, illness (physical or mental) and death experienced as a result of breaking the oath sworn by the victims prior to their journey. One confidential source provided the example of a victim who had recently returned to Nigeria from a country in the region, with assistance from an NGO. After returning, the victim fell ill and died … [S]ources indicated that the victims were convinced that such spiritual attacks were real. In some cases, the sources were also convinced of this. They said that the threat posed by such examples of spiritual attacks was often greater than that posed by physical attacks.’[footnote 147]

12.1.9 According to the 2024 Dutch MoFA note,

‘With regard to the duration of the reprisals or the threat thereof, sources indicated that they ended only when the human traffickers felt that their demands had been met, or when the victim managed to stay out of the hands of the human traffickers.

‘According to confidential sources, victims tried to buy off reprisals whenever possible by entering into instalment agreements with the human trafficker. One source reported that the success of such attempts depended on the human trafficker, but if they did succeed, the repayment period was very short (no more than a few months). There were also instances in which human traffickers continued to threaten with reprisals after the debt had been paid off, in order to prevent victims from cooperating with the criminal prosecution of the human traffickers.

‘Although the criminal prosecution and conviction of human traffickers could sometimes result in victims being further left alone, this was not always the case …

‘… the prosecution and conviction of a human trafficker with the victim’s help could actually serve to increase the risk of reprisals, as the convicted human trafficker might wish to seek revenge. As noted by this source, because convicted human traffickers were often required by the courts to pay financial compensation to their victims, it was also common for human traffickers to want to recover these costs from their victims as well. In addition, according to a confidential source, it was common for victims to fear reprisals even when human traffickers were in prison, as human traffickers rarely work alone.’[footnote 148]

12.2 Family/social attitudes and treatment

12.2.1 The 2023 Dutch MoFA COI report stated:

‘It is difficult to paint a clear picture of society’s views on women who have been exploited in the sex industry in Europe. This is related to the country’s high degree of cultural diversity and the differing profiles of trafficking victims. Nevertheless, victims of sexual exploitation who returned faced the stigma associated with sex work in all parts of Nigeria. It became more difficult for a woman to find a husband, while an unmarried woman has little value in society. The problems were exacerbated if the returning victim was pregnant or had had a child while away from Nigeria. A child was seen as proof of sex work and also meant an extra mouth to feed. Victims were sometimes rejected by their families.

‘Victims who had managed to provide themselves and their families with a decent income experienced fewer problems from this stigma in the south, because the accumulated wealth gave their family more prestige within the wider community. For this reason, victims of sexual exploitation sometimes switched over to exploiting young women themselves.’[footnote 151]

12.2.2 According to the same Dutch MoFA COI report, ‘If a victim was sought by the smugglers or traffickers, the fear of reprisals could be an additional reason for family members not to take her in.’[footnote 152]

12.2.3 The 2024 Dutch MoFA note stated: ‘In some cases, family members themselves were involved [in pressure to pay off debts]. This could be because they had invested money in the journey at the outset; because they had been forced to pay ransom during the journey to free the victim; or because they had hoped to benefit from the income the victim of human trafficking would have generated. In such cases, the mental pressure on the victim to repay debts and generate an income was so great that life in the family circle became traumatising for the victims …’[footnote 153]

12.2.4 Samson Adewumi, a researcher at the University of Zululand, South Africa, in a paper dated June 2024, based on various sources including interviews with 20 ‘low- and middle-class’ female returnees to Nigeria who had migrated for economic reasons[footnote 154], stated:

‘Many migrant women returnees experience a lack of family support, financial insolvency, and unemployment. Respondents explained the challenge of family neglect and support, and how this has made life more difficult for them since their return … In a typical African setting such as Nigeria, there are a lot of expectations from people living overseas. Many family members have become contemptuous of anyone who lives overseas and could not meet up with this expectation … [M]any migrants, including women, go through a lot for survival while overseas and often fall short of these expectations.’[footnote 155]

The paper did not specify whether any respondents had been identified as victims of trafficking but reported that ‘most’ had experienced challenges overseas including sexual harassment and sexual assault, forced and inhumane labour practices, low wages and isolation[footnote 156].

12.2.5 Referring to returnee Nigerian migrants in general, Uzomah and others 2024 stated: ‘Returnees often face stigma from their communities … Some female returnees mentioned being seen as having gone abroad for prostitution, which negatively impacts their access to the labour market and their chances of finding a spouse, as these issues heavily rely on social networks.’[footnote 157] The paper, based on secondary sources and fieldwork including a focus group discussion with men and women who returned to Nigeria during the 10 years to February 2024[footnote 158], did not specify the proportion of female returnees perceived as having been abroad for prostitution. It did not provide information on access to employment or marriageability for those returnees who were not regarded as having done so.

12.2.6 The IOM Regional Office for West and Central Africa, in an undated article on its website about female returnees to Nigeria, including victims of trafficking, reported: ‘In Nigeria, returning with a child often results in family rejection.’[footnote 159]

12.2.7 The 2025 EUAA report stated:

‘Returnees often face stigma from both family and the wider community, resulting in a hostile environment. In some cases, stigma is coupled with the financial burden of repaying debts, which can make safe resettlement in their home communities difficult or even impossible.

‘Family attitudes towards returnees vary widely. Some welcome them with compassion and recognise them as victims of crime, particularly in more informed or urban settings. Others, however, reject or disown them to avoid communal shame, blaming them for leaving or for “bringing shame” through experiences of rape or sexual exploitation. In some cases, returnees are sent away to live elsewhere …’[footnote 160]

12.2.8 The 2025 EUAA report also stated:

‘‘In the Nigerian socio-cultural context, high expectations are placed on individuals living abroad. When returnees, especially women, fail to meet these expectations, they may face resentment, alienation, and even rejection from their families. These culturally driven expectations place added pressure on returnees, contributing to psychological trauma, hindering sense of belonging and their social reintegration.

‘[S]ingle women who lack support network, including divorced women and victims of trafficking, are often perceived by society and even their families as ‘morally questionable’ or ‘loose.’ This perception leads to deep stigma and social exclusion.’[footnote 161]

12.2.9 Citing email correspondence between Morenike Omaiboje, director of Women’s Consortium of Nigeria (WOCON), a Lagos-based NGO[footnote 162], and the EUAA concerning women victims of trafficking, the same EUAA report stated: ‘Women face harsher stigma (especially around ‘sexual shaming, marriageability, and respectability[‘]), which often manifests as social shaming, gossip, and moral judgment directed at survivors. Many returnees from abroad are labelled as sex workers, viewed as having brought dishonour to their families, and are culturally excluded from being considered suitable for marriage.’[footnote 163]

12.2.10 The same EUAA report further stated:

‘Dr Adeyinka noted that “there is persistent and culturally embedded stigma surrounding sex in Nigerian society.” The academic reported that many trafficked women she interviewed were raped, got pregnant and returned to Nigeria with a baby, but they could not disclose that the child was conceived through rape, as the stigma attached to it could ruin both their lives. Instead, “they must constantly lie, saying the father is in Libya or has left them.” Many victims fear that sharing such experiences could later be used against them during conflicts or disputes. The same source added that “this complex situation, where families may depend on returnees for support while simultaneously stigmatising them, shows the contradictory social dynamics surrounding reintegration.”

‘Survivors must navigate both social rejection and strong cultural expectations around family loyalty. As explained by Dr Adeyinka, based on findings of her joint research study[^[164]], even after being trafficked by their own parents, victims continued to send financial support to those same family members. “This reflects a deeply ingrained cultural obligation to honour and support family, regardless of past harm.’ Even when returnees achieve financial success, the stigma may still persist. Individuals who return through forced means often come back empty-handed. In cases where families have taken loans to fund the migration or entered into financial agreements with traffickers, the return results in deeper economic hardship. The burden of repayment falls on the returnees, who are under pressure to find ways to repay debts, often without any resources or support. The Director at Women’s Consortium of Nigeria (WOCON), Morenike Omaiboje, informed that they documented cases in which four families had confined their returning relatives – either siblings or children – upon their arrival. In three other instances, particularly involving siblings, returnees were pressured to repay the money their relatives had contributed towards their initial departure.’[footnote 165]

12.2.11 Referring to the situation of children, the Finnish Immigration Service, in a report on a fact-finding mission to Nigeria in September 2025, cited an interview with a representative at the IRARA’s Abuja office, noting:

‘[R]eturn is particularly difficult for children, who are often born in Europe and experience difficulties adapting to Nigerian society. Often their situation was better in Europe even when they were born there as a result of their mother’s exploitation. This leads to a vicious circle where many victims may want to return to Europe for the sake of their children, even if it means the risk of being trafficked again …’[footnote 166]

12.2.12 Regarding healthcare and psychological support for trafficking returnees, Sarah Adeyinka and Katie Kuschminder, head of the Climate and Migration Division at the United Nations University on Environment and Human Security in Bonn, Germany[footnote 167], published an article in the journal Migration Studies in September 2026, drawing on the 41 interviews conducted in Nigeria with female return migrants as part of the Reintegration project. The article stated:

‘[G]ender violence manifests through medical neglect that treats women’s trafficking-related health conditions as shameful secrets rather than legitimate medical needs requiring specialized care. The silence around reproductive health issues demonstrates how rehabilitation services reproduce patriarchal taboos that render women’s sexual and reproductive trauma invisible, perpetuating rather than resolving the gendered dimensions of trafficking harm.

‘[P]articipants described the complete absence of trauma-informed health and psychological care, despite clear and ongoing consequences of sexual exploitation, detention, and violence. Many suffered from untreated Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), reproductive injuries, and mental health struggles.’[footnote 168]
